transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi. Um, mostly I’m here because I keep… getting up. Like when I’m supposed to just sit and listen, I can’t seem to stay put. During client interviews, tutoring sessions, even my book club—I’ll pop up to get water, check something, move around the room. 

And I’m a private investigator, so you’d think I’d be good at sitting still and observing, right? But people are starting to notice, and it’s embarrassing. I’ll realize halfway through that I’ve been standing by the bookshelf or pacing instead of just sitting in the chair like a normal person.
Do you ever have periods when your mood is unusually high or irritable?

Um… unusually high, like euphoric? I don’t think so. Irritable, sure, sometimes, but I’m not sure it’s in a “period” kind of way. I mean, I can get snappy when I’m stuck waiting or someone’s taking forever to get to the point—actually that happens a lot in interviews, which is funny because my whole job is basically listening to people not get to the point.

But no, I haven’t really noticed stretches where I feel on top of the world or anything like that.
Do you often have trouble staying focused on what someone is saying, even when you want to pay attention?

I mean… maybe sometimes? I’m not sure I’d put it exactly that way. If I want to pay attention, I usually think I am, and then I realize I’m thinking about, like, whether the person’s timeline matches what they said earlier, or why there’s a weird stain on their cuff—sorry, that sounds very detective-y.

But trouble with what they’re saying specifically… I don’t know. People talk in loops a lot, and I can get a little impatient, but I’m not sure if that’s the same as not staying focused.
When you’re sitting and feel like you have to get up, is it usually because you feel anxious or tense?

Not usually anxious, I don’t think. It’s more like… I’m supposed to stay put, and I just don’t. Like in client interviews or tutoring, or even book club, I’ll suddenly be up getting water or standing by a shelf, and then I realize people have noticed. It’s embarrassing because I’m meant to be sitting there listening, but I can’t seem to just stay in the chair.
When you get up like that, do you feel driven to check or do something in a specific way to relieve an urge?

Hmm… I don’t think so? Not like I have to check the door three times or touch something a certain way, if that’s what you mean.

It’s more vague than that. Like I’m up and then I’m doing something—getting water, looking at a bookshelf, moving a chair that’s slightly in the way. Although now that I say “bookshelf,” I do sometimes get distracted by how people organize books, which is probably not what you asked. But no, I don’t think there’s a specific urge I’m trying to relieve.
When you were a child, did teachers or family often describe you as fidgety or unable to stay seated?

Oh, yes. That one is… pretty well documented, unfortunately. My grade-school report cards were basically the same sentence in different handwriting: “bright,” but “doesn’t stay in her seat,” “needs to wait her turn,” that kind of thing.

My mother still brings it up—she says I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through, which is funny now, less funny when you’re the kid being told to sit down for the hundredth time.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about a lot of different things, even when there isn’t a clear reason to?

I don’t know if I’d call it excessive, exactly. I mean, I worry about cases sometimes, or whether I forgot to send an invoice, or whether my neighbor’s tree is going to come down in a storm—which actually, that did happen once, not my neighbor but across the street, and everyone suddenly became an expert in tree roots.

But… sorry, your question was “a lot of different things for no clear reason.” I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed it that way. It’s not the thing that stands out to me.
